text: Banking Fundamentals Educational reference for the BankFlow RAG knowledge base. Core Concepts An account represents a financial relationship between a customer and a bank. A deposit increases the customer's claim on the bank; a withdrawal decreases it subject to available funds and limits. A transfer moves value between accounts. Internal transfers remain within one bank; inter-bank transfers cross bank boundaries. A transaction is a recorded financial operation with an identifier, amount, status, timestamps, parties and audit information. Common Banking Services Account opening and closure, balance inquiry, deposits, withdrawals, electronic transfers, beneficiary management, statements, payment tracking, notifications, fixed deposits and customer support. Account Types Savings accounts are generally designed for personal deposits and withdrawals. Current accounts are commonly designed for frequent business transactions and may have different fee and balance rules. Fixed deposits lock funds for a defined tenure under product-specific terms. Key Terms Available balance: amount currently available for permitted use. Ledger balance: accounting balance represented by posted financial entries. Beneficiary: saved destination account/person. Settlement: finalization of obligations between institutions. Reconciliation: comparison of independent records to identify discrepancies.

Reversal: compensating financial operation used to undo a prior financial effect. Digital Banking Principles Authentication verifies identity; authorization determines permitted actions. Sensitive financial operations require stronger controls than ordinary reads. Money movement should be traceable through financial and audit records. A timeout does not necessarily mean failure; a distributed payment may require status inquiry or reconciliation.

Payments and Transfer Services Reference for payment lifecycles and failure handling. Internal Transfers An internal transfer moves funds between accounts within the same bank and can normally be atomic when both accounts are in one transactional boundary. Both sides of the movement must succeed or neither should commit. Inter-Bank Transfers An inter-bank transfer involves a sending institution, a payment/clearing network and a receiving institution. Typical lifecycle: initiation, validation, authorization, source debit or reservation, network submission, routing, destination processing, acknowledgement, settlement and reconciliation. BankFlow uses a simulated payment network and does not connect to actual NPCI infrastructure. Payment Statuses INITIATED: request created. VALIDATING: request checks are running. DEBITED: source posting completed. SENT: payment submitted to network. CREDIT_PENDING: destination outcome not yet confirmed. CREDITED: destination posting confirmed. COMPLETED: workflow completed. FAILED: payment could not complete. REVERSAL_PENDING: compensation required. REVERSED: source effect compensated. RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED: outcome is ambiguous and needs investigation. Failure Scenarios Network timeout can leave remote state uncertain. Duplicate requests require idempotency keys. Destination unavailability may require retry, reconciliation or reversal.

Acknowledgement loss can occur after the receiving side has actually succeeded. Payment Rails — Conceptual Instant payment systems prioritize rapid account-to-account transfer. NEFT-like systems can be modeled as electronic transfers with defined processing/settlement behavior. RTGS-like systems model real-time gross settlement concepts for eligible transactions. BankFlow models concepts only and does not reproduce production protocols. Beneficiaries Production systems may apply verification, cooling periods, transfer limits and additional authentication. BankFlow can simulate these controls.

BankFlow Product and Service Manual Ground-truth reference for the simulated application's capabilities. Customer Services Registration, login, profile management, multiple accounts, deposits, withdrawals, internal transfers, inter-bank transfers, beneficiary management, transaction history, statements, notifications and payment tracking. Account Services Create, view, freeze, unfreeze and close accounts subject to authorization and state rules. Balances use integer minor units. The financial ledger is the accounting source of truth. Transfer Service Internal and inter-bank transfers use idempotency keys so retries do not create duplicate effects. Inter-bank workflows can enter pending, timeout, reversal or reconciliation states. Admin Services Authorized administrators can view users, inspect accounts, freeze/unfreeze accounts, inspect transactions and payment states, review reconciliation mismatches and inspect audit events. Notifications Email, SMS and push notifications are simulated asynchronously and are never the source of financial truth. Boundaries BankFlow is an educational simulation. It does not provide actual payment-network connectivity, regulatory certification, real KYC/AML processing or real-world financial guarantees. The AI assistant must not invent undocumented BankFlow features.

Distributed Banking Systems and Payment Architecture Reference for microservices, ledger, concurrency and distributed reliability. Microservices Each service owns a bounded business capability and its data. BankFlow separates authentication, users, accounts, ledger, transactions, payments, beneficiaries, banks, settlement, reconciliation and notifications. Services communicate through APIs and asynchronous events rather than querying another service's database. ACID Transactions Atomicity means a financial operation commits completely or not at all. Consistency preserves database constraints and business invariants. Isolation controls concurrent interaction. Durability means committed data survives normal failures. Concurrency PostgreSQL row-level locking such as SELECT ... FOR UPDATE can serialize modifications to the same account state. Optimistic locking can use a version number to detect concurrent modifications. Isolation levels include READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE. Double-Entry Ledger Every balanced journal has equal total debits and credits. The ledger provides an auditable accounting trail; balance projections must remain consistent with it. Event-Driven Architecture Kafka can carry durable domain events such as payment completion, ledger posting, settlement and reconciliation. Consumers should be idempotent because delivery can repeat.

tecture Kafka can carry durable domain events such as payment completion, ledger posting, settlement and reconciliation. Consumers should be idempotent because delivery can repeat. RabbitMQ can handle background work such as notifications and statement generation. Transactional Outbox A service writes its database state change and an outbox event in one transaction. A publisher later delivers the event to Kafka. This prevents a successful database commit from being separated from event publication. Saga and Compensation A distributed transaction can be decomposed into local transactions coordinated by a Saga. If a later step fails, compensation corrects earlier effects. Compensation preserves history rather than deleting financial records. Caching and Locks Redis can provide caching, rate limiting, sessions and selected distributed coordination. Redis is not the financial source of truth; PostgreSQL and the ledger are authoritative.

Consistency Financial posting should be strongly consistent within its transaction boundary. Notifications, analytics and read projections may be eventually consistent. Failure Modes Partial failure occurs when one service succeeds while another fails. Timeout creates uncertainty about remote state. Duplicate delivery requires idempotent consumers. Reconciliation resolves disagreements between systems.
